name: eight queens, 2,056 placements
hook: There are {choose} ways to put {n} queens on a chessboard. Backtracking finds every solution after placing {placed}.
caption: Place n queens on an n by n board so that no two share a row, a column or a diagonal.
The naive way chooses any {n} of the {cells} cells and validates the whole board only once a full placement is proposed. That is {choose} candidates.

First prune: no two queens can share a row, so each row gets exactly one, and the only choice is which column. Second: check a placement before making it. Along one diagonal direction row - col is constant, along the other row + col is, so three sets answer 'is this square attacked?' in O(1).
Choose, explore, unchoose: {placed} queens placed, all {solutions} solutions found. A dead end is abandoned at the first conflict, with everything that would have been built on top of it.
What was the first backtracking problem that clicked for you? 👇
cta: The capstone of the module, after Subsets, Permutations and Generate Parentheses.

p: Each needs a pairwise check, and the whole board is validated only once a full placement is proposed.
No two queens can share a row, so each row gets exactly one. The choice at each level is *which column*.
Along one diagonal direction `row - col` is constant. Along the other, `row + col` is.
So keep three sets: used columns, used `row - col`, used `row + col`. A placement is legal exactly when all three are absent.
Three O(1) lookups instead of a scan over every queen placed so far.
